slides.title: Learning Outcome
slides.text:
Learning Outcome
•  Learn about redundant & closed-chain structures
•  Understand robot actuation schemes, transmission systems, and actuator
   selection principles.
•  Analyze stiffness, deflection, and compliance effects in robotic manipulators.
•  Explain position and force sensing techniques used in robotic systems.

•  Understand workspace, trajectory, and kinematic
   considerations in mobile manipulation systems.





                                                                                                           2

visualInspection.notes: Five outcome bullets: redundant/closed chains, actuation/transmission/selection, stiffness/compliance, position/force sensing, mobile manipulation workspace/trajectory/kinematics.

slides.title: Redundant & Closed-chain Structures - Micromanipulators
slides.text:
Redundant & Closed-chain Structures - Micromanipulators :
•  Redundant manipulators, which possess more than the minimum six degrees
   of freedom (DOF) required for general spatial positioning and orienting.
•  Closed-chain structures: where links form one or more closed loops.
•  Micromanipulators: A micromanipulator consists of several fast, precise DOF
   located at the distal end (near the tool) of a conventional manipulator.
•  Singularity Avoidance: Additional joints allow a mechanism to avoid singular
   configurations.
•   Collision Avoidance:
    – A 6-DOF robot can reach a specific position and orientation in
        only a finite number of ways.
    – A 7-DOF manipulator provides an infinity of solutions for any
       given pose, allowing the controller to select a configuration
        that avoids obstacles in cluttered environments.

                                                                                                           3

visualInspection.notes: Redundancy stated as more than six DOF for full spatial pose; closed loops; distal fast precise micromanipulator DOFs; extra joints help singularity/collision avoidance. The universal 6-DOF finite-solutions and 7-DOF infinite-solutions-for-any-pose claims require reachable regular poses, rank/task/limits qualifiers. Redundancy is task-relative, not always n>6.

slides.title: Closed-loop structures
slides.text:
Closed-loop structures :                     End effector (Moving Platform)

•  Unlike serial chains, closed-loop structures
   connect links in a circuit.
•  The Motoman L-3 robot possesses closed-loop
   structures in the drive mechanism of joints 2
   and 3.
•   Stiffness: The primary benefit of closed-loop                  Base
   structures is increased mechanical stiffness.                                                   Closed Loop
•  Workspace: closed-loop structures generally
   reduce the allowable range of motion of the
    joints and thus decrease the workspace size
   compared to serial linkage.




                                                                                                           4

visualInspection.notes: Closed-loop versus serial topology; Motoman L-3 joints2/3 named; increased stiffness versus generally smaller joint range/workspace. Right schematic labels moving end-effector upper platform, base below and dashed closed-loop route; three drawn struts illustrate topology, not proof of six actuators or a Motoman L-3 image.

slides.title: The Stewart Mechanism
slides.text:
The Stewart Mechanism :

•  The Stewart mechanism is a fully parallel 6-DOF manipulator.
•   It consists of a base and an end-effector platform
   connected by six linear actuators.
•   Joint Configuration: Each actuator is connected
   to the base via a 2-DOF universal joint and to the
   end-effector via a 3-DOF ball-and-socket joint.
•  Inverse kinematics is simple because actuator lengths are calculated directly
   from the platform's position and orientation.
•  Whereas forward kinematics is highly complex and often
   has no closed-form solution.
•  They provide very high stiffness and load-carrying capacity,
   but their workspace and range of motion are limited.

                                                                                                           5

visualInspection.notes: Six linear actuators connect base and moving platform; each leg base universal joint2DOF, platform spherical joint3DOF. Fully parallel6DOF, easy inverse length computation versus complex forward pose recovery, high stiffness/load capacity and limited workspace. Right photo shows actual six-leg platform. Inverse length derived as norm(p+Rbi−ai), not printed; “often no closed-form” not a categorical impossibility.

slides.title: Grübler’s Formula
slides.text:
Grübler’s Formula :

•  To determine the actual Degrees of Freedom (DOF) of a complex or closed-loop
   mechanism, Grübler’s Formula is used:
  ➢𝐹= 6 𝑙−𝑛−1 + σ𝑖=1𝑛   𝑓𝑖
    – 𝐹→ total DOF in the mechanism,
    – 𝑙→ total number of links (including the base),
    – 𝑛→ total number of joints,
    – 𝑓𝑖→ DOF of the 𝑖𝑡ℎjoint
•  Stewart Mechanism Example :
•  Step 1: Number of Joints
  ➢6 Universal Joints → 6 × 2 = 12 DOF
  ➢6 Ball-and-Socket Joints → 6 × 3 = 18 DOF
  ➢6 Prismatic Joints → 6 × 1 = 6 DOF
  ➢𝑛= 18

                                                                                                           6

visualInspection.notes: Exact formula F=6(l−n−1)+Σ fi. l counts links including ground; n counts joints. Counts six universal2DOF, six spherical3DOF, six prismatic1DOF, n18. The formula assumes independent generic constraints; singular/special overconstrained cases need rank analysis. Photo repeats the platform, no new dimensions.

slides.title: Stewart Mechanism Example (Continued)
slides.text:
Stewart Mechanism Example : (Continued)

•  Step 2: Number of Links
   ➢12 actuator links
  ➢1 fixed base
  ➢1 moving platform
  ➢𝑙= 14
•  Step 3: Sum of Joint Freedoms
  ➢σ 𝑓𝑖= 6 × 2 + 6 × 3 + 6 × 1 = 36
•  Applying Grübler’s Formula: 𝐹= 6 𝑙−𝑛−1 + σ𝑖=1𝑛   𝑓𝑖
  ➢𝐹= 6 14 −18 −1 + 36
  ➢𝐹= 6 −5 + 36  → 𝐹= 6



                                                                                                           7

visualInspection.notes: Twelve actuator links (two rigid members per telescoping actuator), one base, one platform =>l14. Sum fi12+18+6=36. F=6(14−18−1)+36=6. Continued photo no new geometry; numerical derivation is substantive incremental content.

slides.title: Actuation Schemes - Actuator location
slides.text:
Actuation Schemes - Actuator location :

•  Once the kinematic configuration is finalized, the designer must address the
   actuation of the joints.
•   In robotics, the actuator, the speed-reduction system, and the transmission
   system are closely coupled and must be designed as an integrated unit.
•  The choice of actuation scheme fundamentally dictates the manipulator's
   dynamic performance, controllability, and structural efficiency.
•  There are two primary philosophies regarding where an actuator should be
   placed relative to the joint it drives:
    –  Direct-Drive Configuration: The actuator is located at or
       near the joint, and its output is attached directly to the joint.
    – Remote Actuation: The actuator is located toward the base
        of the manipulator, away from the joint it drives.


                                                                                                           8

visualInspection.notes: Integrated motor, reducer and transmission design; effects on dynamic performance, control and structure. Local direct drive: actuator at/near joint output attached directly; remote drive toward base away from driven joint. Proximity alone is not sufficient to call a geared motor direct drive; use stated direct-output connection.

slides.title: Reduction and transmission systems
slides.text:
Actuation Schemes - Reduction and transmission systems :
•  Gears : Gears are the most common elements for speed
   reduction, providing high ratios in compact packages.
•  Types: Spur gears, bevel gears, worm gears, or cross helical gears.
•  Disadvantages: They introduce backlash and friction.
•  Tight meshing to eliminate backlash often increases friction.
•  The relationships between input  𝑖 and output 𝑜parameters are:
                       ሶ𝜃𝑖  ➢ ሶ𝜃𝑜=            𝜂

   ➢𝜂: Gear ratio (speed-reducing and torque-increasing factor)
  ➢𝜏𝑜= 𝜂𝜏𝑖 (For speed-reduction systems, we define: 𝜂> 1)
   ➢Where, ሶ𝜃𝑖, ሶ𝜃𝑜: Input and output speeds
    ➢𝜏𝑖, 𝜏𝑜: Input and output torques

                                                                                                           9

visualInspection.notes: Spur, bevel, worm, cross-helical gears named and pictured (photos are unlabelled individually); backlash/friction; tighter mesh trades less backlash for more friction. η>1 is speed-reduction ratio, not efficiency. ωo=ωi/η and τo=ητi require ideal lossless magnitudes or consistent sign convention; actual friction acknowledged above makes unconditional exact torque equation incomplete.

slides.title: Flexible Bands, Cables, and Belts
slides.text:
Actuation Schemes - Flexible Bands, Cables, and Belts

•  These systems are used for remote transmission and can combine transmission
   with reduction.
•  Here the flexibility is proportional to the length of the element.
•  Because they only work in tension, they require preloading or opposing active
   systems to stay engaged on pulleys.
•  Toothed Belts and Roller Chains: Offer higher stiffness and compactness; roller
   chains can bend around smaller pulleys
•  Gear Ratio in Pulley Systems
              𝑟2   – 𝜂=
              𝑟1                              𝑟1                   𝑟2
   –  𝑟1, 𝑟2: Radii of the input and output pulleys,
        respectively.

                                                                                                          10

visualInspection.notes: Remote transmission and possible reduction; flexibility proportional to element length under unchanged material/section; tension-only requires preload or opposing active drive. Toothed belts and roller chains described as stiffer/compact, chains around smaller pulleys (qualitative comparisons need fixed design basis). Diagram small input r1 left, larger output r2 right, open belt; η=r2/r1, no slip implied, opposite ratio would be speedup.

slides.title: Lead Screws and Ball-Bearing Screws
slides.text:
Actuation Schemes - Lead Screws and Ball-Bearing Screws :
•  These transform rotary motion into linear motion
   with large reduction in a compact package.
•  Lead screws : operate by having the internal              Nut            Race
   threads of a nut ride directly on the external
   threads of a screw. Transform rotary motion into
    linear motion.
•  Lead Screws: Very stiff, support large loads,
                                                                              Ball-Bearing   but high friction.                               Lead Screw[1]
                                                                 Screw [1]•  Ball-Bearing Screws: Instead of direct thread-on-thread
    contact, ball-bearing screws utilize a recirculating circuit
   of ball bearings located between the sets of threads.
•  Ball-Bearing Screws: Use recirculating ball bearings to
   reduce friction; they are typically back drivable.


                                                                                                          11

visualInspection.notes: Rotary-to-linear conversion. Left drawing direct lead-screw/nut thread contact labelled Nut; right drawing balls between threads labelled Race. Lead screws stiff/high load/high friction; ball screw recirculating bearings reduce friction and are typically backdrivable, not always self-locking. No lead/pitch equation printed; derived kinematics only if explicitly supplied.

slides.title: Stiffness and Deflections
slides.text:
Stiffness and Deflections:

•   In the design of high-performance robotic manipulators, maintaining the overall
    stiffness of the structure and the drive system is a critical engineering objective.
•  Most industrial manipulators do not have sensors to measure the tool frame
   location directly; instead, they rely on forward kinematics calculated from
   sensed joint positions.
•    If the links or transmission systems are compliant,
   the manipulator will sag under gravity or other loads,
   leading to inaccurate tool positioning.
•  Furthermore, mechanical flexibilities in the structure or
   drive train lead to resonances, which impose severe
   limitations on the manipulator's dynamic performance
   and control bandwidth.


                                                                                                          12

visualInspection.notes: Structural and drivetrain stiffness important. Source says most industrial robots infer tool pose via forward kinematics of sensed joint positions; do not present survey claim as timeless fact. Compliance yields sag under gravity/load and rigid-model pose error; flexibility produces resonances limiting dynamic performance/control bandwidth. Encoders alone may miss unmodelled link deformation.

slides.title: Flexible elements in parallel and series
slides.text:
Stiffness and Deflections-Flexible elements in parallel and in series :

•  To analyze the total stiffness of a complex manipulator assembly, we model
   individual components as springs.
•   Parallel Connection: For two flexible members of stiffness 𝑘1and 𝑘2connected
    in parallel, the net stiffness is:  𝑘parallel = 𝑘1 + 𝑘2
•  Series Connection: For two flexible members connected in series, the net
                       1      1    1
    stiffness is:      =  +
                     𝑘series   𝑘1   𝑘2
•   In a robot's transmission, different stages of reduction
   are typically in series. This means the total compliance
   (the reciprocal of stiffness) is the sum of the individual
   compliances.




                                                                                                          13

visualInspection.notes: Parallel k=k1+k2; series1/k=1/k1+1/k2; compliance reciprocal. For reduction stages in series, stiffness/compliance must first be referred to the same coordinate/shaft using p592; raw numbers on different shafts cannot be directly summed. Scalar linear-spring model, positive k, common generalized coordinate.

Stiffness and Deflections – Shafts and Gears
•  Shafts : Shafts are fundamental for transmitting rotary motion from motors to
    links. Their torsional stiffness is a major contributor to the overall drive-train
    flexibility.
•  The torsional stiffness 𝑘 of a round shaft is:
           𝐺𝜋𝑑4
  ➢𝑘=
               32𝑙
      where 𝑑: Shaft diameter 𝑙: Shaft length and 𝐺: Shear modulus of elasticity
•  Gears : Gears provide torque multiplication but introduce compliance into the
   drive system.
•  The stiffness of an output gear (with the input gear fixed)
   can be estimated as:
• 𝑘= 𝐶𝑔𝑏𝑟2  where 𝑏: Face width of the gears , 𝑟: Radius of
   the output gear and 𝐶𝑔: Material constant.

                                                                                                          14

visualInspection.notes: Solid round shaft torsional k=Gπd^4/(32l), d diameter not radius, l length G shear modulus. Gear output stiffness with input fixed k=Cg b r², b face width r output radius Cg material constant. Both rotational units N·m/rad, not N/m. Shaft and gear photos contain no dimensions; avoid inferring tooth counts. Formula assumes uniform linear-elastic solid shaft; hollow shaft needs polar difference not supplied.

slides.title: Electric Motors
slides.text:
Electric Motors :

•   Electric motors are widely used due to easy interfacing and precise control.
•  They have lower power-to-weight ratios than
    fluid actuators but are ideal for precision robotics.
•  DC Brush Motors : The DC brush motor is the most
   straightforward actuator to control.
•   It operates by conducting current to the windings of the rotor via stationary
   brushes that maintain contact with a revolving commutator.
•  The primary limiting factor is the overheating of the
   windings.
•  Torque output is proportional to the current conducted
   to the rotor windings via brushes and a commutator.


                                                                                                          16

visualInspection.notes: Electric motors easy interface/precision; qualitative power-weight comparison with fluids; DC brushed motor stationary brushes feed rotor windings through rotating commutator. Winding overheating major limit; torque proportional current for constant flux/linear model. Generic motor cutaway at upper right does not explicitly show labelled brushes/commutator, so do not identify DC topology from photo alone.

slides.title: Position Sensing
slides.text:
Position Sensing :

•   Virtually all modern industrial manipulators are designed as servo-controlled
   mechanisms.
•   In this architecture, the control law generates a force or torque command to
   the joint actuators based on the error signal.
•  The error signal is the difference between the desired joint position and the
   actual position sensed by internal feedback devices.
•  The most effective design strategy is the use of co-located sensor and actuator
    pairs, where the position sensor is located directly
   on the shaft of the actuator.





                                                                                                          17

visualInspection.notes: Servo control uses desired-minus-sensed joint position error to generate force/torque command. Co-located sensor at actuator shaft is recommended. “Most effective” not a universal end-effector-accuracy guarantee; shaft sensing can miss downstream compliance p589. No sensor hardware diagram. Modern-industry prevalence claims should be source-attributed.

slides.title: Force Sensing
slides.text:
Force Sensing :

•  Force sensors measure contact forces between the
   manipulator end-effector and the environment
   using strain gauges.
•   Strain gauges are bonded to metal structures
   and produce outputs proportional to strain.
•  Important design considerations include
   sensor count, sensor placement, structural
    stiffness, sensitivity, and overload protection.
•  Force sensors are commonly placed at joint
   actuators, wrist joints, and end-effector fingertips.
•  Wrist sensors typically measure 3–6 components of the
   force–torque vector acting on the end-effector.

                                                                                                          18

visualInspection.notes: Strain-gauge contact force sensors: bonded to metal, output proportional strain in calibrated range. Design count/placement/stiffness/sensitivity/overload; positions actuator/wrist/fingertips; wrist3–6 wrench components. Photo shows cylindrical transducer and enlarged serpentine bonded foil gauge with two leads; do not infer total gauge count or six-axis capability from one pictured gauge. Not all possible force sensors use gauges; scope to illustrated class.

slides.title: Force Sensor Design Issues
slides.text:
Force Sensor Design Issues :

•  Force sensing relies on measuring flexure deflection; therefore, higher stiffness
   reduces sensitivity.
•  Overload protection is achieved using limit stops to prevent excessive flexure
   deformation.
•  Eliminating hysteresis is important and is achieved by minimizing welded or
   bolted joints near flexures.
•   Differential measurements improve linearity and reduce temperature and off-
    axis disturbances
•   Foil strain gauges are durable but less sensitive, while
   semiconductor gauges provide much higher sensitivity
   but are more prone to overload damage.



                                                                                                          19

visualInspection.notes: Flexure deflection creates stiffness-versus-sensitivity tradeoff; limit stops protect overload; minimizing welded/bolted joints near flexures reduces hysteresis (does not prove eliminates all hysteresis). Differential measurements improve linearity and reject shared temperature/off-axis effects under suitable arrangement, not all arbitrary differential pairs. Foil more durable/lower sensitivity; semiconductor higher sensitivity/more overload vulnerability; comparison as given.

slides.title: Mobile Robots
slides.text:
Mobile Robots :

•  Mobile robotics is an interdisciplinary field integrating mechanical, electrical,
   and electronics engineering with computer, cognitive, and social sciences.
•   It focuses on the technology of mobility,
   enabling a robot to move unsupervised through
   real-world environments to perform tasks.
•  Unlike fixed manipulators, mobile robots can
  move throughout a facility and perform tasks flexibly at different locations.
•  To achieve robust mobility, a robot must integrate
   several different "modules" or layers of competence.
•  A successful design requires the fusion of knowledge
   from kinematics, signal analysis, information theory,
    artificial intelligence, and probability theory.

                                                                                                          20

visualInspection.notes: Interdisciplinary mechanical/electrical/electronics/computer/cognitive/social sciences; autonomous mobility focus versus fixed arms; multiple competence layers; kinematics, signal analysis, information theory, AI, probability. Small four-wheel top-view schematic no dimensions or drive labels. Do not identify drive type from icon alone, or define every mobile robot as necessarily unsupervised.

slides.title: Locomotion
slides.text:
Locomotion :

•  Locomotion is Fundamental Challenge and the complement of manipulation.
•  While manipulation involves a fixed robot moving objects,
   locomotion involves a fixed environment and a robot
   moving by imparting force to that environment
•  Legged Locomotion: Bio-inspired locomotion using
   articulated limbs with gait-controlled motion.
•  Gait Control: Sequence of leg lift and release
   events in walking robots.
•  Wheeled Locomotion: Common mobile robot mechanism
   including differential, synchro, and omnidirectional drives.
•  Some advanced robots use active COM shifting to climb
   obstacles several times the diameter of their wheels

                                                                                                          21

visualInspection.notes: Locomotion moves robot by forces against environment; source contrasts fixed-arm object manipulation. Legged locomotion uses articulated limbs and gait leg-lift/release sequence; differential/synchro/omnidirectional wheel drive names. Active COM shift may enable obstacle climbing beyond wheel size, not unconditional numerical guarantee. Drawings show biped stick figure and generic four-wheel icon, no detailed drive geometry.

slides.title: Wheeled Mobile Robots
slides.text:
Wheeled Mobile Robots

•  The wheel is the most popular locomotion mechanism in mobile robotics due to
    its high efficiency on flat ground and relatively
   simple mechanical implementation.
•  Unlike legged robots, wheeled robots are generally
   designed so all wheels maintain ground contact at
    all times, making balance less of a research priority;
•  Three wheels are typically sufficient for static stability.
• We focuses on traction, stability, maneuverability, &control.
•  The Design Space : A roboticist must simultaneously
   consider wheel type and arrangement (geometry), as
   these choices dictate the robot’s performance in three
   key areas: stability, maneuverability, and controllability.


                                                                                                          22

visualInspection.notes: Wheels efficient on flat ground and mechanically simple; general all-wheels-contact design and lower balance emphasis, not universal. Three wheels typically suffice for static stability only with noncollinear supports and COM projection inside support polygon; slope/dynamic forces can change result. Design focus traction/stability/maneuverability/control. Photo has four wheels and payload; no kinematic drive identification justified.

slides.title: Wheel Geometry
slides.text:
Wheel Geometry :

•  The selection of wheel types and their arrangement, referred to as wheel
   geometry,
•  They are central to the design of a mobile robot’s locomotion mechanism.
•  These choices directly affect robot maneuverability, controllability, and stability.
•  Mobile robots use diverse wheel configurations to adapt to different operating
   environments and applications.
•  No "Ideal" Configuration: There is no single configuration that simultaneously
   maximizes all three characteristics.
•  A designer must choose the most appropriate drive
   configuration based on the unique constraints and
   environmental niche of the specific application



                                                                                                          23

visualInspection.notes: Wheel type plus arrangement determine wheel geometry and influence stability, maneuverability, controllability. No universally ideal configuration; choose based on environment/task constraints. Repeats some p599 ideas but adds explicit no-single-optimum application-specific tradeoff.

slides.title: Mobile Robot Workspace and Degrees of Freedom
slides.text:
Mobile Robot Workspace and Degrees of Freedom

•  The workspace of a mobile robot defines the range of possible poses (positions
   and orientations) the robot can achieve within its environment.
•  Robot Pose: On a horizontal plane, the pose of a robot chassis is represented by
   a vector of three elements: its x and y coordinates
    in a global reference frame and its angular orientation 𝜃.
•  Total Degrees of Freedom (DOF): While a robot may      Environmen
   have many internal joints, the rigid body of the robot        t
   chassis on a 2D plane has exactly three degrees of freedom.





                                                                                                          24

visualInspection.notes: Workspace is attainable poses; planar chassis coordinates x,y,theta in global frame; exactly three rigid planar pose DOFs independent of internal joint count. Do not equate three configuration coordinates to three independently commandable instantaneous velocities for nonholonomic wheels. Right ellipse labelled Environment (word linebreak cosmetic), car icon and star obstacles; not all drawn region necessarily collision-free or reachable.

slides.title: Mobile Manipulation
slides.text:
Mobile Manipulation :

•  Mobile manipulation involves mounting a manipulator arm on a mobile robot
   chassis to overcome the "lack of mobility" inherent in
   standard industrial robot arms.
•  Manipulation involves a fixed robot moving objects
   within its workspace by imparting force to them.
•  Whereas locomotion involves a fixed environment
   where the robot moves by imparting force to that
   environment.

•  Gross Motion vs. Fine Motion: A significant advantage of
   mobile manipulation is the ability to use the mobile robot
   chassis for gross motion while the arm performs fine
    tasks.

                                                                                                          25

visualInspection.notes: Arm mounted on mobile chassis extends reach; chassis gross motion versus arm fine tasks. Illustrated arm with gripper mounted on blue wheeled base; no exact DOF count justified by stylized joints/two visible wheels. Contrast of fixed-arm manipulation versus robot locomotion is illustrative, not a ban on simultaneous mobile manipulation.

slides.title: Summary
slides.text:
Summary

•  Robot design integrates actuation, transmission, sensing, stiffness, and control
   systems.
•  Mobile robots achieve autonomous mobility through locomotion, perception,
    localization, cognition, and navigation.



•  Mobile manipulators combine base mobility with robotic
   manipulation for expanded workspace and flexible task
   execution.
•   Effective mobile manipulator design requires proper
   base selection, stability management, and configuration-
   space path planning.

                                                                                                          26

visualInspection.notes: Integrated actuation/transmission/sensing/stiffness/control. Adds explicit autonomy modules locomotion, perception, localization, cognition, navigation and effective mobile design base selection, stability management, configuration-space planning. Not merely excluded summary: these named topics need coverage. Mobile base plus arm expands workspace/flexibility but obstacles/limits remain.

sourceIssues.finding: Redundancy is described using six DOF, and finite/infinite pose-solution counts are stated without reachability, rank or joint-limit qualifications.
sourceIssues.handling: Use task-relative rank and reachable regular full-pose assumptions; extra freedom can aid avoidance but does not guarantee it.

sourceIssues.finding: The spatial mobility formula is introduced as giving actual DOF without its independence qualification.
sourceIssues.handling: Keep the correct Stewart arithmetic and state the generic independent-constraint assumptions; do not infer universal singularity-free mobility.

sourceIssues.finding: Exact torque multiplication is printed without a lossless qualification despite nearby friction discussion.
sourceIssues.handling: Retain the ratio convention, explicitly state ideal magnitudes, and derive a separately labelled efficiency variant from power balance.

sourceIssues.finding: Reduction stages are described as series compliances without stating that they must first be referred to a common shaft.
sourceIssues.handling: Apply p592’s η² stiffness transformation before combining rotational compliances; raw values from different coordinates cannot simply be added.

sourceIssues.finding: The unqualified most-effective co-location recommendation can be mistaken for guaranteed tool-pose accuracy.
sourceIssues.handling: Distinguish actuator-coordinate feedback from downstream elastic displacement and use p589 as the explicit qualification.

sourceIssues.finding: Minimizing welded/bolted joints is worded as eliminating hysteresis.
sourceIssues.handling: Ask about reducing a contributing source, not proving zero hysteresis. Differential cancellation is tested only under explicit matched-channel assumptions.

sourceIssues.finding: Three wheels and generally maintained contact can be misread as unconditional stability guarantees.
sourceIssues.handling: State level-ground, noncollinear-contact and COM-support conditions; keep traction, dynamic loads and unusual wheel layouts distinct.
